noteBlocks.lede: Millions of carbon compounds exist, and you never learn them one at a time. Carbon's four bonds build chains of any length, and the chains fall into families whose members step up by one CH₂. Learn a family's rules and you know its members.

noteBlocks.md: There are millions of carbon compounds, far too many to learn one by one, and you do not have to. They sort into families, and every member of a family follows the same rules, so the rules of one family cover members you have never met. This topic is the first family: the alkanes.

noteBlocks.md: Every carbon atom forms **four covalent bonds**: no more, no fewer. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons, drawn as one line. A carbon can bond to other carbons and still have bonds to spare, so carbon atoms join into chains of any length, with hydrogen on the spare bonds. That is why there are so many carbon compounds, and why sorting them into families makes them manageable.

noteBlocks.caption: Count the lines at a carbon: four is right. Five, or three, is a drawing of something that cannot exist.

noteBlocks.stem: Hydrogen forms one covalent bond and carbon forms four. Explain why carbon can build chains of any length but hydrogen cannot. [3]

steps.working: A carbon atom has four bonds to make, so it can join to another carbon and still have three bonds left.
steps.decision: Start from the number of bonds: it decides what an atom can join to.

steps.working: A carbon at the end of a chain still has bonds to spare, so another carbon can always be added: the chain can keep growing.
steps.decision: A chain grows only if the atom at its end has a bond to spare.

steps.working: Hydrogen has only one bond. Once it has joined something it has none left, so it can only cap the end of a chain.
steps.decision: Say what the other atom cannot do: hydrogen ends a chain and never extends one.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student draws a carbon atom with five lines coming from it. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: carbon forms four bonds, so one line is too many
nothing: carbon can form as many bonds as there is room for
carbon forms two bonds, so three lines are too many
noteBlocks.answer: carbon forms four bonds, so one line is too many
noteBlocks.explain: Carbon forms exactly four covalent bonds, so a fifth line cannot be there. Counting the lines at every carbon, as step 1 of See it counts the bonds a carbon has to make, is how you check any structure you draw.

optionNotes.option: nothing: carbon can form as many bonds as there is room for
optionNotes.why: Carbon's number of bonds is fixed at four; room on the page makes no difference to it.

optionNotes.option: carbon forms two bonds, so three lines are too many
optionNotes.why: Two bonds belongs to oxygen. Carbon forms four, so only one line is extra here.

twin.prompt: Another drawing shows a carbon atom with only three lines coming from it. What is wrong?
options: one bond is missing: carbon needs four
nothing: three bonds is enough for a carbon
one line is too many: carbon forms two bonds
twin.answer: one bond is missing: carbon needs four
twin.explain: Carbon needs four bonds, so a carbon with three lines has one missing. Step 1 of See it starts from this: a carbon always has four bonds to make.

optionNotes.option: nothing: three bonds is enough for a carbon
optionNotes.why: Three is one short. Every carbon in a structure you draw must show four lines.

optionNotes.option: one line is too many: carbon forms two bonds
optionNotes.why: Carbon forms four bonds, not two, so the drawing needs one more line, not one fewer.

noteBlocks.title: Why some carbon compounds are no family
noteBlocks.md: Methane, ethanol and ethene all contain carbon, but they are not one homologous series: they have three different general formulae and react in different ways. A family needs all four features at once. You need the alkanes' names only up to butane; the longer ones below are here for their numbers.

steps.working: Every formula fits one general formula, CnH2n+2: pentane has 5 carbons and 2 × 5 + 2 hydrogens, and the same holds on every row.
steps.decision: Test the general formula on every row, not just one.

steps.working: Each formula is one carbon and two hydrogens more than the one before it: they differ by CH₂.
steps.decision: Compare neighbours: the step between them is the feature.

steps.working: The boiling points rise steadily, 36, 69, 98 and 126 °C: a gradation in a physical property.
steps.decision: Read the trend from the data and name it with the specification's word, gradation.

steps.working: All four have only C–C and C–H single bonds, so they react in the same kinds of way: similar chemical properties.
steps.decision: Chemical properties come from the bonds, and the bonds are the same kind in every member.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Chemistry - Hydrocarbons - Alkanes & Homologous Series
noteBlocks.why: A second run through the family, the general formula and the names, beside our own worked steps.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two alkanes differ by C₂H₄. Could they be next to each other in the series?
options: no: neighbours differ by one CH₂ only
yes: any difference in carbon and hydrogen will do
yes: C₂H₄ is the step between neighbours
noteBlocks.answer: no: neighbours differ by one CH₂ only
noteBlocks.explain: No. Neighbours differ by exactly one CH₂, as step 2 of See it found row by row. C₂H₄ is two CH₂ steps, so another member sits between them.

optionNotes.option: yes: any difference in carbon and hydrogen will do
optionNotes.why: The step is fixed at one carbon and two hydrogens. A bigger gap means a member is missing in between.

optionNotes.option: yes: C₂H₄ is the step between neighbours
optionNotes.why: C₂H₄ is two CH₂ groups together, so it spans two steps, not one.

twin.prompt: Which pair could be next to each other in the alkanes?
twin.explain: C₁₄H₃₀ is one carbon and two hydrogens more than C₁₃H₂₈: one CH₂, the step that step 2 of See it found between neighbours.

optionNotes.why: That gap is C₂H₄, two CH₂ steps, so one member is missing between them.
Same number of carbons with two fewer hydrogens is not the CH₂ step, and C₁₃H₂₆ does not fit CnH2n+2.

noteBlocks.md: A **hydrocarbon** is a compound (or molecule) that consists of **hydrogen and carbon only**. Without the word *only*, the sentence also fits ethanol, which has oxygen as well. Every alkane is a hydrocarbon, but not every hydrocarbon is an alkane: an alkene such as propene is a hydrocarbon too.

noteBlocks.title: The definition earns two marks
noteBlocks.md: One mark for **carbon and hydrogen atoms**, one for **only**. Call them atoms: the 2025 reports record marks lost where they were called ions or molecules.

noteBlocks.stem: Which of these are hydrocarbons: C₇H₁₆, C₂H₅OH, CCl₄ and C₃H₆? Give a reason for each. [4]

steps.working: C₇H₁₆ has carbon and hydrogen and nothing else: a hydrocarbon, and an alkane.
steps.decision: Read the elements from the formula, then ask whether anything besides C and H is there.

steps.working: C₂H₅OH also has oxygen, in the OH: not a hydrocarbon.
steps.decision: One extra element rules a compound out: that is the word only at work.

steps.working: CCl₄ has carbon and chlorine but no hydrogen: not a hydrocarbon.
steps.decision: Both elements must be there; carbon with anything else does not count.

steps.working: C₃H₆ has carbon and hydrogen only: a hydrocarbon, but not an alkane, because 2 × 3 + 2 is 8, not 6.
steps.decision: Hydrocarbon is about which elements; alkane is about the formula as well.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a hydrocarbon?
noteBlocks.explain: C₅H₁₀ contains carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon, even though it is not an alkane (step 4 of See it). CH₃OH has oxygen too, and CO₂ has no hydrogen.

optionNotes.why: It has carbon and hydrogen, but the O is oxygen as well, so it is not hydrogen and carbon only.
It has carbon but no hydrogen at all, and a hydrocarbon needs both elements.

twin.prompt: Which of these is NOT a hydrocarbon?
twin.explain: C₂H₅Cl has chlorine as well as carbon and hydrogen, so it fails the word only, as step 2 of See it showed for oxygen.

optionNotes.why: C₈H₁₈ is carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon; it is an alkane too.
C₄H₈ is carbon and hydrogen only, so it is a hydrocarbon, even though it is not an alkane.

noteBlocks.text: 4. The alkanes and their general formula

noteBlocks.md: The **alkanes** are the hydrocarbons with the general formula $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$: for **n** carbon atoms there are **2n + 2** hydrogen atoms. They are **saturated**: every bond is a single bond. To use the formula, **double the carbons, then add two**, and write the finished formula with one number after each element. A formula left as a sum earns nothing.

noteBlocks.stem:
(a) Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 15 carbon atoms. [1]
(b) An alkane has 78 hydrogen atoms. How many carbon atoms does it have? [1]

steps.working: (a) Hydrogens = 2 × 15 + 2 = 32.
steps.decision: Double the carbons first, then add the two end hydrogens.

steps.working: (a) The formula is C₁₅H₃₂, with the sum finished.
steps.decision: One number after each element: C₁₅H₃₀₊₂ is a rule, not a formula.

steps.working: (b) Work backwards: take off 2, then halve. (78 − 2) ÷ 2 = 38 carbons.
steps.decision: Undo the steps in reverse order: the 2 went on last, so it comes off first.

steps.working: (b) Check forwards: 2 × 38 + 2 = 78, so the alkane is C₃₈H₇₈.
steps.decision: A backwards answer is only safe once you have run it forwards.

noteBlocks.prompt: An alkane has 17 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
noteBlocks.explain: 2 × 17 + 2 = 36: double the carbons, then add two, as step 1 of See it did for 15 carbons. The alkane is C₁₇H₃₆.

twin.prompt: An alkane has 19 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have?
twin.explain: 2 × 19 + 2 = 40, the same two moves as step 1 of See it: C₁₉H₄₀.

noteBlocks.md: The first four alkanes are named by their number of carbons: **meth** 1, **eth** 2, **prop** 3, **but** 4, and every name ends **-ane**. A **molecular formula** counts the atoms. A **structural formula** (a displayed formula) shows **every atom and every bond** as a line.

To draw one, draw the carbon chain first, then add hydrogens until every carbon has four lines. An end carbon is joined to one carbon, so it carries three hydrogens; a carbon inside the chain is joined to two, so it carries two.

steps.decision: Chain first. An alkane is saturated, so every carbon-to-carbon bond is single.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student draws a chain of six carbon atoms and puts three hydrogen atoms on every carbon. What is wrong?
options: the four inside carbons can carry only two hydrogens each
nothing: three hydrogens on each carbon is right
the end carbons should carry four hydrogens each
noteBlocks.answer: the four inside carbons can carry only two hydrogens each
noteBlocks.explain: An inside carbon is joined to two carbons, so only two of its four bonds are spare, as step 2 of See it found for pentane. Three hydrogens would give it five bonds.

optionNotes.option: nothing: three hydrogens on each carbon is right
optionNotes.why: Count to four at an inside carbon: two bonds to carbons and three to hydrogens makes five, one too many.

optionNotes.option: the end carbons should carry four hydrogens each
optionNotes.why: An end carbon already uses one bond on its neighbour, so it has room for three hydrogens, not four.

twin.prompt: Another student draws the same six-carbon chain with two hydrogen atoms on every carbon. What is wrong?
options: each end carbon needs three hydrogens
nothing: two hydrogens on each carbon is right
the inside carbons need three hydrogens each
twin.answer: each end carbon needs three hydrogens
twin.explain: An end carbon is joined to only one carbon, so three of its bonds are spare, as step 2 of See it found. With two hydrogens it shows only three bonds.

optionNotes.option: nothing: two hydrogens on each carbon is right
optionNotes.why: Count to four at an end carbon: one bond to a carbon and two to hydrogens is only three.

optionNotes.option: the inside carbons need three hydrogens each
optionNotes.why: An inside carbon already uses two bonds on its neighbours, so two hydrogens is right for it.

noteBlocks.text: 6. Why boiling points rise, and states

noteBlocks.md: Along the family the molecules get bigger, and bigger molecules attract each other more strongly. More energy is needed to pull them apart, so the **boiling point rises** with each CH₂: that is the gradation.

For a **state at room temperature (20 °C)**, compare 20 °C with the melting and boiling points. Below the melting point it is a solid; between the two, a liquid; above the boiling point, a gas. Methane, ethane, propane and butane all boil below 20 °C, so all four are **gases**.

noteBlocks.stem: Pentane melts at −130 °C and boils at 36 °C. What is its state at 20 °C? Explain your answer. [2]

steps.working: 20 °C is above pentane's melting point, −130 °C, so it has already melted.
steps.decision: Compare with the melting point first: above it, the solid has gone.

steps.working: 20 °C is below its boiling point, 36 °C, so it has not boiled: pentane is a liquid.
steps.decision: Between the melting and boiling points means liquid. Name the state and give the comparison: that is the mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: An alkane with 20 carbon atoms melts at 37 °C and boils at 343 °C. What is its state at 20 °C?
noteBlocks.explain: Solid: 20 °C is below its melting point, 37 °C, so it has not melted. Make the melting-point comparison first, as step 1 of See it did.

optionNotes.why: A liquid needs 20 °C above the melting point, and 37 °C is higher than room temperature.
It boils at 343 °C, far above room temperature, so it cannot be a gas at 20 °C.

twin.prompt: Heptane melts at −91 °C and boils at 98 °C. What is its state at 20 °C?
twin.explain: Liquid: 20 °C is above −91 °C and below 98 °C, so heptane has melted but not boiled, the two comparisons of steps 1 and 2 of See it.

optionNotes.why: A gas needs 20 °C to be above the boiling point, and 98 °C is far above room temperature.
A solid needs 20 °C to be below the melting point, but −91 °C is far below it.

noteBlocks.md:
Five ways a right idea loses its mark:
**1.** Name the **family** from its formula: CnH2n+2 alkanes, CnH2n alkenes, CnH2n+1OH alcohols. Not one member, such as ethene.
**2.** Write a **finished formula**: work out 2n + 2 and put one number after the H, never a sum.
**3.** A structural formula shows **every bond**: each H needs its own line.

**4.** In the hydrocarbon definition, carbon and hydrogen are **atoms**, not ions or molecules.
**5.** Chemical properties are **similar**, not the same and not different, and the step between members is **CH₂**, not CH₃.

noteBlocks.title: What the reports record
noteBlocks.md: The Summer 2025 C2 reports record the CnH2n family named as the alkanes or as ethene, the twelve-carbon alkane left with its arithmetic unfinished, and the hydrocarbon definition losing *only* or calling the atoms molecules or ions. In 2023 few saw that four small alkanes were all gases.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that an alkane with n carbon atoms has 2n + 2 hydrogen atoms. [4]

steps.working: Each carbon has four bonds, so n carbons have 4n bond ends between them.
steps.decision: Count what is available before counting what is used.

steps.working: A straight chain of n carbons has n − 1 carbon-to-carbon bonds, and each uses two bond ends, one from each carbon: 2(n − 1) ends.
steps.decision: Joining things in a line always takes one link fewer than the number of things.

steps.working: The ends left over each hold one hydrogen: 4n − 2(n − 1) = 4n − 2n + 2 = 2n + 2.
steps.decision: Subtract the ends used from the ends available, then open the bracket with care.

steps.working: So the formula is CnH2n+2. For one carbon it gives 2 × 1 + 2 = 4 hydrogens: methane, as it should.
steps.decision: Test a proof on the smallest case you already know.

noteBlocks.prompt: Use the same counting for a straight chain of 40 carbon atoms. How many carbon-to-carbon bonds join them?
noteBlocks.explain: 39: one bond fewer than the number of carbons, as step 2 of See it said, because 40 atoms in a line need 39 links.

twin.prompt: For that chain of 40 carbons, how many bond ends are left for hydrogen?
twin.explain: 4 × 40 = 160 ends, minus 2 × 39 = 78 used: 82 left, the subtraction of step 3 of See it. That is 2 × 40 + 2.

noteBlocks.stem: An alkane has a relative formula mass of 86. Find its molecular formula. [3]

steps.decision: Write the general Mr as an equation with the value you are given.

steps.working: Take off 2, then divide by 14: n = (86 − 2) ÷ 14 = 6.
steps.decision: Undo the operations in reverse order.

steps.working: 6 carbons and 2 × 6 + 2 hydrogens: C₆H₁₄. Check: 6 × 12 + 14 × 1 = 86.
steps.decision: Always check by working the Mr forwards from your formula.

noteBlocks.prompt: An alkane has a relative formula mass of 114. How many carbon atoms does it have?
noteBlocks.explain: 8: take off 2 and divide by 14, as step 2 of See it did. (114 − 2) ÷ 14 = 8, so the alkane is C₈H₁₈.

twin.prompt: Another alkane has a relative formula mass of 212. How many carbon atoms does it have?
twin.explain: 15: (212 − 2) ÷ 14, the reverse steps of step 2 of See it. The alkane is C₁₅H₃₂.

noteBlocks.md:
give the four features of a **homologous series**: same general formula, similar chemical properties, a gradation in physical properties, a CH₂ step.
define a **hydrocarbon** as a compound of hydrogen and carbon atoms **only**.
use $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ forwards and backwards, and write the finished formula.
name methane, ethane, propane and butane, draw each by counting to four, and say all four are **gases**.
find a state by comparing 20 °C with the melting and boiling points.

Organic chemistry has been Question 4 of the C2 paper at both tiers every summer since 2023. It opens with a definition or a general formula, asks you to name a family or finish a formula, and ends with a structure or a state. Draw the chain first, count to four at every carbon, and write *only* in the hydrocarbon definition. The Sheet lists the traps.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a feature of a homologous series?

options.text: successive members differ by a CH₃ group
options.feedback: They differ by CH₂, not CH₃. One more carbon brings two more hydrogens with it.

options.text: they have the same general formula
options.feedback: That is one of the four features, so it is not the odd one out.

options.text: they show similar chemical properties
options.feedback: That is a real feature: the same bonds mean the same reactions.

options.text: their physical properties show a gradation
options.feedback: That is a real feature, and the boiling-point graph is the picture of it.

items.stem: What is the general formula of the alkanes?

options.text: CnH2n+2
options.feedback: Double the carbons and add two. It works for every alkane, however long.

options.text: CnH2n
options.feedback: That is the alkenes. The two extra hydrogens are what a double bond costs.

options.text: CnH2n+1OH
options.feedback: That is the alcohols, which carry an OH group. The alkanes have no functional group at all.

options.text: CnHn+2
options.feedback: The carbons are doubled first. For butane, 2 × 4 + 2 = 10 hydrogens, not 6.

items.stem: An alkane has 12 carbon atoms. What is its molecular formula?

options.feedback: 2 × 12 + 2 = 26. Work the arithmetic out and write the finished formula.
That is CnH2n, the alkene rule. An alkane needs the extra two hydrogens.
That adds 2 to the carbon count without doubling it first. Double, then add.
That is the rule half-applied. Summer 2025 examiners report exactly this: finish the arithmetic and write one number.

options.text: a compound consisting of hydrogen and carbon only
options.feedback: Both halves are marks: what it contains, and the word only.

options.text: a compound containing hydrogen and carbon
options.feedback: Without only, ethanol fits the description and it is not a hydrocarbon. That missing word is reported as a lost mark every year.

options.text: a molecule made only of carbon
options.feedback: Carbon on its own is graphite or diamond. A hydrocarbon needs hydrogen too.

options.text: a compound of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen only

items.stem: How many hydrogen atoms are in the displayed formula of propane?

options.feedback: Three on each end carbon and two on the middle one: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8.
That gives every carbon two hydrogens. The end carbons have a spare bond each, so they take three.
That gives every carbon three. The middle carbon is joined to two other carbons, so it has only two bonds left.
Ten belongs to butane, which has four carbons. Propane has three.

items.stem: The first four alkanes boil at -162, -89, -42 and -1 °C. What is their state at room temperature, 20 °C?

options.text: all four are gases
options.feedback: Every one boils below 20 °C, so at room temperature all four have already boiled.

options.text: all four are liquids
options.feedback: A substance is liquid between its melting and boiling points. All four boil well below 20 °C, so they are past that already.

options.text: methane is a gas and the rest are liquids
options.feedback: Compare each boiling point with 20 °C: butane's -1 °C is still below it, so butane is a gas too.

options.text: it cannot be worked out from boiling points
options.feedback: It can, and this is how the exam asks it: above its boiling point a substance is a gas.

items.stem: Why do the alkanes have similar chemical properties?

options.text: they contain the same kinds of bond, so they react in the same ways
options.feedback: Same bonds, same reactions. Only the chain length changes along the family.

options.text: they have the same boiling point
options.feedback: Their boiling points differ, and that difference is the gradation in physical properties — a separate feature.

options.text: they all have the same number of carbons
options.feedback: The carbon count is what changes from one member to the next. The bonding is what stays the same.

options.text: they all have a functional group
options.feedback: Alkanes have no functional group, which is exactly why they are the least reactive family here.

items.stem: What does a displayed formula show that a molecular formula does not?

options.text: the relative formula mass
options.feedback: Neither formula shows the Mr; you work that out from the Data Leaflet.

options.text: the state at room temperature
options.feedback: No formula shows the state. You get that from the boiling point.

prompts.prompt: Why do boiling points rise as you go along the alkane family?
prompts.answer: Each member has one more CH2, so the molecules are larger and attract each other more strongly, and more energy is needed to separate them.

prompts.prompt: How many hydrogens would you draw on the middle carbon of any alkane chain, and why?
prompts.answer: Two, because it has already used two of its four bonds joining the carbons on either side of it.

findings.asked: Pick three features of a homologous series, name the family with general formula CnH2n, give the formula of a twelve-carbon alkane, and define a hydrocarbon.
findings.wentWrong: CnH2n was widely taken for the alkanes, or answered with a single compound's name. The twelve-carbon formula was sometimes left with its arithmetic unfinished. The definition of a hydrocarbon lost the word 'only', or called the carbon and hydrogen molecules rather than atoms.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the two general formulae apart, finished the arithmetic before writing the formula, and put the word 'only' into the definition.
findings.rule: Alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n; a hydrocarbon is hydrogen and carbon only.

findings.asked: The same definition of a hydrocarbon at Higher, with the identification of a homologous series from its general formula.
findings.wentWrong: The definition again lost 'only', and some answers described the carbon and hydrogen as ions.
findings.rule: A hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

findings.asked: Read four structures: which are gases, which is an alkane, name a four-carbon alkene, then draw butane.
findings.wentWrong: Few worked out that all four were gases; the structure of butane was drawn poorly; the names were confused with each other.
findings.rule: Count the carbons for the prefix, draw every bond as a line, and compare each boiling point with room temperature.

findings.asked: Organic chemistry across the whole section, including the physical state of propane.
findings.wentWrong: Giving the state of propane defeated many candidates, even with its boiling point in front of them.
findings.rule: Compare the boiling point with room temperature: below it means a gas.

findings.asked: Name and give the formula of organic compounds from their structures, write a general formula, and give a physical state.
findings.wentWrong: Only a few gave the general formula correctly, and only a few gave the physical state; the structure of propene was poorly drawn.
findings.rule: Learn CnH2n+2 for the alkanes, and read a state from the boiling point against room temperature.

insight.ruleToRemember: A homologous series shares a general formula, shows similar chemical properties and a gradation in physical properties, and steps by CH2. Alkanes are CnH2n+2, saturated, and the first four are gases; a hydrocarbon is hydrogen and carbon only. Draw the carbon chain first and add hydrogens until every carbon shows four bonds.
insight.aStarSignal: Moving freely between the name, the molecular formula and the displayed formula of any member, and using the general formula on a chain far beyond the four that are named.
